subtype: Approach: learning from last year's trip and adjusting [Revision]
passage: Last year on the trip to the science park, my small bottle was empty by noon. My mouth felt like paper and I had to ask Hemant for sips, which made me feel bad. So this time I packed the big steel bottle. Amma said it was heavy, but I said I would rather be heavy than thirsty. I also told Hemant, "Bring a big one too, it gets really hot there." He laughed but agreed. At noon we sat in the shade, both bottles still half full, and I remembered last year and smiled. - Sonali

qa.q: Why did Sonali have to ask Hemant for sips last year?
qa.a: Sonali's small bottle was empty by noon.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel about asking Hemant for sips last year?
qa.a: Sonali felt bad about it, and that memory pushed the change to a bigger bottle.

qa.q: What other approach could Sonali use to make sure water lasts through a hot day, and why?
qa.a: Sonali could ask the teacher where taps are on the route and top up there, so the day does not depend on one bottle.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Sonali's advice to bring a big bottle?
qa.a: He laughed, so it may seem a bit fussy at first, but at noon his bottle is half full too, which suggests the advice was sensible.

grounding: A child recalls being thirsty on last year's trip and changes the plan with a bigger bottle and a word to a friend.

subtype: Approach: staying put and waiting to be found [Thinking]
passage: The lantern festival market in Kyoto was so crowded that Jana lost her mother's sleeve in the noodle queue. She turned in a circle. Faces, elbows, bags. Her legs wanted to run. Then she remembered the rule from school: lost children stop moving. "If I go, Mum won't know where to look. If I stay, she will come back the way we walked." She stepped beside a pillar near the paper-lantern stall, where she had last held her mother's hand, and waited with her fingers pressed together. After a few minutes her mother, Aiko, pushed through the crowd, breathless, and hugged her tightly.

qa.q: Where did Jana wait for her mother?
qa.a: She waited beside a pillar near the paper-lantern stall.

qa.q: What was Jana feeling when she first turned in a circle?
qa.a: Panicked, since her legs wanted to run and she could see only faces, elbows and bags.

qa.q: What else could Jana do if her mother has not come after a while, and why?
qa.a: She could ask a stall owner with a fixed spot to help find her mother, since staying put and asking a safe helper work well together.

qa.q: How might Aiko feel as she searches back along the route?
qa.a: Frightened and hurried at first, then relieved, as her breathless push through the crowd and tight hug show. 🤍

grounding: A girl separated from her mother stops moving because the searching parent will look back along the route.

subtype: Approach: asking a safe helper such as a shopkeeper or uniformed person [Action]
passage: At the temple fair in Wadgaon, the crowd swallowed Francis's father somewhere between the bangle stall and the swings. Francis looked left and right. The balloon seller kept drifting; the woman with a cart was leaving. But at the gate stood a policeman, and beside him a tea shop with a tin roof that never moved. Francis walked to the shop, where Pema Aunty was stirring milk. "Aunty, my name is Francis D'Souza. My father's name is Joseph D'Souza." He gave the phone number slowly, one digit at a time. "Please call him, or say it on the loudspeaker." She reached for the phone.

qa.q: What details did Francis tell the shop owner?
qa.a: He said his own name, his father's name and the phone number.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling while he waited beside the counter?
qa.a: Anxious but steady, because he had picked a fixed shop and said everything clearly.

qa.q: What other approach could Francis use if the tea shop could not help, and why?
qa.a: He could go to the policeman at the gate, who stands at a fixed post and can make an announcement.

qa.q: How does Pema Aunty see Francis's request?
qa.a: She sees a boy who says his name, his father's name and the number clearly, so she can act quickly.

grounding: A child picks a fixed shop or a uniformed person, states names and number clearly, and asks for a call or announcement.

subtype: Approach: following the first friendly adult who offers to help [Pitfall]
passage: Chinmay's mother had vanished behind a stack of clay pots at the weekly market in Sirsi. His chest tightened and tears blurred everything. "Beta, lost?" said a man with a friendly smile. "Come, I saw your mother go this way." Chinmay nodded and let himself be led past the vegetable rows, past the bus stand, farther and farther from the pot stall where his mother had said to meet. At the far gate Vishal, a fruit seller, frowned. "Whose boy is this?" The man's smile went thin and he hurried off. Vishal kept Chinmay at his cart and phoned his mother. Waiting there, Chinmay realised he had never asked the man a single question.

qa.q: Where did the man lead Chinmay?
qa.a: He led him past the vegetable rows and the bus stand to the far gate.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when the man offered to help?
qa.a: Panicked and desperate for relief, since tears blurred everything and he nodded at once.

qa.q: What could Chinmay have done instead of following the man, and why?
qa.a: He could have stayed near the pot stall and asked a shopkeeper with a fixed stall to call his mother, because a friendly voice alone is no proof of trust.

qa.q: How does Vishal see the man and the boy?
qa.a: Vishal senses something is wrong, since the man hurries off when asked, so he keeps the boy safe at his cart and phones his mother.

grounding: A boy panics and goes off with a friendly stranger without checking, and ends up far from the meeting spot.

subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of a lost-child plan made beforehand [Thinking]
passage: Before we went into the Sunday bazaar, Papa crouched and asked me, "Tanmay, if we get separated, what will you do?" I felt silly but said it aloud, counting on my fingers: stop, find a shop, say the number, stay in the same area. Didi Shalini made me say it twice, once faster. Amma's number I already knew by heart. Later, in the crush by the spice stalls, I lost sight of Amma and my stomach dropped. Then the four steps came into my head one after another, and I was already stopping. Amma found me beside the spice shop a minute later. - Tanmay

qa.q: What four steps did Tanmay say aloud before the bazaar?
qa.a: Tanmay said: stop, find a shop, say the number and stay in the same area.

qa.q: How did Tanmay feel when Amma disappeared from sight?
qa.a: Scared, since Tanmay's stomach dropped, but steadier once the four steps came to mind.

qa.q: What could strengthen the plan for next time, and why?
qa.a: The family could also agree on a meeting spot, so both Tanmay and the parents know exactly where to head.

qa.q: Why might Didi Shalini have made Tanmay say the plan twice?
qa.a: Didi Shalini probably wanted Tanmay ready to say it even when rushed, so Didi Shalini asked for a second, faster try.

grounding: A family rehearses a lost-child plan aloud beforehand, so the child can use it when separated in a crowd.

passage: Hemant let go of his father's hand for one second to look at a kite, and when he looked up the bazaar was all strangers' legs. His heart thudded. He closed his eyes. "Where was I holding his hand? The sweet shop with the jalebi pans. And the blue gate next to it." He reasoned that Papa would look back along the way they had come, and the sweet shop was the one place they both knew. So he walked, not ran, past two stalls, stopped by the blue gate and stood still. Sunaina Aunty from the sweet shop noticed and handed him a stool. Soon his father's checked shirt came through the crowd.

qa.q: Which two landmarks did Hemant remember?
qa.a: He remembered the sweet shop and the blue gate.

qa.q: What was Hemant thinking as he closed his eyes to recall the way?
qa.a: He was calming himself and working out where he had last held his father's hand.

qa.q: What else could Hemant do if his father does not come soon, and why?
qa.a: He could ask Sunaina Aunty to phone his father, because a shop owner at a fixed spot is an easy, safe helper.

qa.q: How might Hemant's father look for him?
qa.a: His father would probably retrace their steps too, going to where they were last together, so the landmark gives them a good chance to meet.

grounding: A boy recalls the landmarks near where he last held his father's hand and calmly returns to them.

subtype: Approach: running in panic through the lanes [Pitfall]
passage: From my uncle's shoe stall I saw a boy of about ten sprinting between the lanes, head twisting left and right. His mother, Dolma, I learned later, was running the opposite way, calling his name. The lanes bend, so each time one of them turned a corner the other had already gone through. Once he nearly hit a pole and I called, "Do you know your father's number?" He opened his mouth and only gasps came out. I can't tell what he was thinking; maybe he was too scared to think at all. In the end my uncle stepped into the middle of the lane and waved them both over. - Himani

qa.q: What happened when the narrator asked the boy for his father's number?
qa.a: He opened his mouth and only gasps came out.

qa.q: What might the boy have been feeling as he ran?
qa.a: Terrified, probably, since he was too scared to think and could not even say a number he knew.

qa.q: What could the boy try instead of running, and why?
qa.a: He could stop, breathe and ask a shopkeeper to call, because staying put lets his parents find him and calm lets him remember the number.

qa.q: How does the search look from Dolma's side?
qa.a: Dolma is frightened and calling his name, and because she also keeps moving, each turn takes her past him.

grounding: A child sprints through lanes in panic while the parents also move, so they keep missing each other.

passage: The Thursday market in Pala roared with sellers and scooters, and Latha could not see her aunt's green sari anywhere. Her eyes burned. A wail was starting in her throat. Instead she stepped back until her shoulders touched a shop wall. In, she told herself, slowly, and out. She counted to ten with her fingers pressed on her thigh. By seven the roar seemed to shrink. By ten she could read the sign over the nearest shop: hardware, with a man in a blue lungi behind the counter. That shop isn't going anywhere, she thought. She walked in. "Uncle, I'm Latha. Please help me find my aunt." Jomon Chettan reached for his phone.

qa.q: What did Latha do to calm herself against the wall?
qa.a: She breathed slowly and counted to ten.

qa.q: What was Latha feeling before she stepped back to the wall?
qa.a: Frightened and close to tears, since her eyes burned and a wail was starting in her throat.

qa.q: What could Latha do while waiting, and why might it help?
qa.a: She could stay by the wall or shop where her aunt might return and keep her breathing slow, because a fixed spot is easy to find.

qa.q: How does Jomon Chettan see a girl who walks in and speaks up?
qa.a: He sees a calm, clear child who gives her name and her need, so he can help right away and phones.

grounding: A girl feeling tears rising breathes slowly against a wall, counts to ten, then picks a shopkeeper to approach.

subtype: Approach: switching from wandering to staying and asking [Revision]
passage: Paulo had already walked two lanes of the Sunday market in Singapore's Little India, and every stall looked the same: flowers, bangles, phone covers. His family was at none of them. Each corner took him farther from where they had started, and his throat felt tight. He stopped short. "I keep moving and they keep not being here." Beside a chai stall he planted his feet, took a breath and looked up at the owner, a woman named Ada. "Please, can you call my father? I'm lost." Ada wiped her hands and picked up her phone. Paulo sat on an upturned crate and watched the crowd, this time only waiting.

qa.q: Where did Paulo stop to ask for help?
qa.a: He stopped beside a chai stall.

qa.q: What was Paulo thinking when he stopped short?
qa.a: He realised his walking was making things worse, since each corner took him farther from his family.

qa.q: What could Paulo have done from the start, and why?
qa.a: He could have stayed near the place he last saw his family and asked a stall owner for help, because his family would come back there.

qa.q: How might Ada see Paulo's request?
qa.a: She sees a boy who asks politely and clearly, so she can act at once by picking up her phone.

grounding: A boy who wanders and makes things worse switches to staying and asking a stall owner to phone his father.

subtype: Approach: fixed meeting point agreed in advance [Action]
passage: Come, sit, and I will tell you about the day your cousin Kiran got lost at the fair. Before we went in, I told the boy, "If we lose each other, come to the temple gate. Do not wander." Then, near the sweet stalls, the crowd pushed us apart. I stood at the gate with my heart in my mouth, staring at every small head. And there he came, marching straight from the lane, with a shopkeeper pointing the way behind him. I am Aadhya, his aunt, and I have never been so glad to see a proud face. He had not cried once. The plan had told him where to go.

qa.q: Where had Aadhya and Kiran agreed to meet if they lost each other?
qa.a: They agreed to meet at the temple gate.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling as she waited at the gate?
qa.a: Worried, with her heart in her mouth, and then very glad when Kiran appeared.

qa.q: What choice did Kiran make that kept him safe?
qa.a: He went straight to the agreed place and let a shopkeeper point the way, instead of wandering about.

qa.q: How did Kiran see the plan Aadhya had given him?
qa.a: He trusted it, since the plan told him where to go and let him get there without crying.

grounding: A family agrees a meeting point beforehand, so the lost child walks straight to it with a shopkeeper's directions.
